opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the natural way to picture it is closer to how a human programmer actually works, rather than this one-shot "sample a program and hope it's right" paradigm. When you look at an ARC task, you don't usually get the full transformation in one go. You form a partial hypothesis — "okay, it looks like the objects are being recolored based on their size" — you write a little bit of code for that, you run it on the training examples, and then you look at where it fails.

And that's the key part: the execution feedback. You've got these input-output pairs, so you can actually run your candidate program and see the diff between what it produced and what it should have produced. Maybe it gets three out of four examples right, or maybe it gets the colors right but the positions wrong. That's an incredibly rich signal, and a system should be able to look at that and say, "Ah, I missed that the largest object is treated differently," and then revise the program rather than throwing it away and starting over.

So you can imagine a loop where a model, say a language model that's been fine-tuned or prompted to write programs, proposes an initial program, executes it, observes the outputs, and then conditions on that feedback to propose an edit. You can treat it as a search over edits, a kind of tree, where you keep the promising branches and prune the ones that aren't converging. There's a real tradeoff there, actually, between spending your compute budget on lots of independent fresh samples versus spending it on deep refinement chains, and empirically it's not obvious which wins. Often you want some mix of the two: breadth to get diverse starting hypotheses, depth to polish the ones that are almost there.

The other thing I'd love to see, and this connects to work we've done on library learning like DreamCoder, is that iteration shouldn't just happen within a single problem. Across many ARC problems you start to discover recurring concepts: object segmentation, symmetry, gravity-like movement, counting. If the system can pull those out into reusable abstractions, then the next time it iterates on a problem it's working in a richer language, and the edits it needs to make become shorter and more meaningful. So you get this nice two-level iteration: refine programs within a task, and refine the library across tasks.

I think that combination of neural intuition for proposing and revising code, symbolic execution for grounded feedback, and an accumulating library of abstractions is really the promising recipe for something like ARC.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model proposing and revising programs with execution feedback, but does not communicate a sequence of an induction model followed by a transduction model.

r002.rationale: It proposes repeatedly executing the current program on examples, inspecting the outputs and failures, and using that feedback to revise the next code-writing step.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that when a person sits down with an ARC problem, they almost never get it right in one shot. You look at the examples, you form a hypothesis, you check it against the grids, and it's wrong in some specific way. Maybe you got the color rule right but the shape got rotated the wrong direction, or you handled the first two examples but the third one breaks it. And then you don't throw everything away and start over. You keep the parts that worked and you patch the part that didn't.

So an iterative programming approach would try to mimic that loop. You have a model, say a language model, that proposes a program, some actual code that maps input grids to output grids. You run that program on the training examples. Now you have something really valuable, which is concrete feedback: here's the output your program produced, here's what it should have produced, here's the diff. That diff is extremely informative. It tells you roughly where the hypothesis is broken. Then you feed that back in and ask the model to revise the program, and you go around again.

What I like about this is that it turns a search problem into something more like a debugging problem. Pure sampling, where you just generate thousands of programs and hope one of them passes, treats every attempt as independent. But the failures aren't independent, they're structured. A program that gets ninety percent of the pixels right is probably close to a correct program in some sense, and you want to exploit that. Iteration lets you climb toward the solution rather than hoping to land on it.

There are a couple of things that make this hard, though. One is that the model has to actually understand the execution feedback, not just see it as more tokens. It needs to connect "the output has an extra row at the bottom" to "I'm iterating one past the boundary in this loop." That kind of causal reasoning from program behavior back to program text is something humans are decent at and models are getting better at, but it's not free. The second thing is that you can get stuck. You make a local fix, it breaks something else, you fix that, and you oscillate. So you probably want some combination of iterative refinement and breadth, where you keep a few diverse candidates alive and refine them in parallel, rather than committing to a single lineage.

And then the piece I find most interesting is whether you can learn to iterate better. If you collect lots of these trajectories, programs, their failures, and the fixes that worked, you can train on them. The model starts to learn not just what good ARC programs look like, but what good edits look like given a particular kind of error. That's much closer to how expertise actually works. An expert programmer isn't someone who writes perfect code the first time, it's someone who recognizes their mistakes quickly and knows how to repair them.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model proposing and revising programs, but does not specify applying an induction model and a transduction model in sequence.

r002.rationale: It proposes running the current program on training examples and using the resulting errors to guide the next revision.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d want a loop where you propose a program, run it on the examples, and then use what went wrong to guide the next proposal. So you’re not asking the model to look at the grids and produce a perfect program in one shot. You’re giving it an opportunity to experiment.

Suppose your initial hypothesis is that you should identify an object and move it to the right. You execute that, and perhaps it gets one example right but fails on another. Now you can ask: Did I select the wrong object? Is the movement relative to another object, rather than a fixed number of pixels? Those are different kinds of revisions, and the execution results can help distinguish them.

The interesting question is how to make that feedback useful. Just saying ‘your program is wrong’ doesn’t tell you very much. Showing the predicted grid alongside the target, or letting the system inspect intermediate objects, gives it more structure to reason about.

But ultimately, matching the examples isn’t enough. There are lots of programs that could do that. You want to find a compact explanation that captures the underlying rule and therefore has a chance of working on the test input. So I imagine combining a learned model that proposes and revises programs with an explicit search process that checks them.

r001.rationale: The response describes a learned model proposing and revising programs alongside explicit search, but it does not propose applying induction and transduction models in sequence.

r002.rationale: It proposes a loop that runs a program on examples and uses the failures to guide the next proposal, which communicates evaluation informing the next code-writing step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the natural approach is to treat it as a search over programs, where you don’t expect to get the program right on the first try. You propose a hypothesis about the transformation, write a little program that implements it, and run that program on the examples. Then you look at where its predictions disagree with the outputs and use those disagreements to revise the hypothesis.

So perhaps your first hypothesis is, “Find this object and move it to the right.” But when you execute it, you discover that it works on one example and fails on another. That failure might tell you that you’ve identified the wrong object, or that the displacement depends on some other feature of the scene. The important thing is that execution gives you a very concrete form of feedback.

The challenge is making that feedback useful for search. A system needs to reason about whether it should make a small change to the program or abandon the interpretation altogether. And because ARC gives you very few examples, matching those examples isn’t sufficient by itself. You also need a preference for explanations that are simple and coherent, so that the program captures the underlying rule and generalizes to the test input.

r002.rationale: It says to run the current program on examples, use prediction disagreements as feedback, and revise the hypothesis and program accordingly.
